newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels poise for round seven of crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels poise for round seven of crisis talks.

text.p: As Peru's government and Marxist rebels were poised on Thursday to resume talks to end the 10-week Lima hostage siege, a guerrilla leader asserted time was on the rebels' side and congressmen vowed to probe the crisis.

The government and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) were slated on Thursday to hold a seventh round of preliminary talks aimed at bloodlessly ending the siege at the Japanese ambassador's home.
After a sixth round on Tuesday, guarantors overseeing the talks said only that the two sides met "in the same atmosphere" as prior meetings, which it had described as "constructive."
An MRTA leader, meanwhile, said time was on the rebels' side and that guerrillas were prepared to wait as long as necessary for a "dignified solution to the siege."

"We are in no hurry. We have time on our side," a rebel who identified himself as Comrade Alejandro, a member of the MRTA's high command, told Reuters at a secret training camp in Peru's central jungle.
"What do we lose if we wait months, when we have waited centuries for a revolution?"

Congress President Victor Joy Way said lawmakers have before them six proposals to create a panel to investigate why Peru's security forces failed to prevent the MRTA from seizing the diplomatic compound.
"We are going to take this up immediately after the incident at the Japanese embassy is resolved," Joy Way told reporters.
Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer, meanwhile, reiterated the hostages were generally in good shape although the health of two of them was "delicate."

While no details were given of Tuesday's sixth round of talks, Peruvian and Japanese officials expressed optimism progress has been made since face-to-face discussions restarted on Feb. 11 and were upbeat ahead of Thursday's seventh session.
"We have expectations that Thursday's meeting will signify a step forward," said Jorge Santistevan, Peru's public defender. "Not even a fly's buzz should interrupt these negotiations."

The rebels seized the mansion on Dec. 17, taking hundreds of VIPs hostage. All but 72 mostly middle-aged men -- including Fujimori's brother, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia and two government ministers -- were still being held as crisis entered its 72nd day.
Rebels are demanding the release of up to 400 jailed comrades. The government has rejected the demand. Neither side has shown it has given ground.
Comrade Alejandro said rebel leader Nestor Cerpa's presence at talks starting last week showed the government was "starting to give ground."
But President Alberto Fujimori also claims patience to see through the hostage crisis, already the longest in Latin America's history, and has made no sign of shifting his position.

"We hope there is an accord that benefits both sides," Alejandro said, adding the MRTA would be satisfied only with a "dignified" solution to the siege. Such a solution would mean either a bloody end where Peruvian security forces stormed the fortified compound or, in the case of a peaceful outcome, one where "the morale of the movement remained high," he added.
If the MRTA did win the release of its jailed comrades, the movement's leader, Victor Polay, would not take up arms again and would work instead for a lasting peace, his mother said.

"If my son should get out of prison, he would feel an urgent need to rejoin his family," Otilia Campos de Polay told Reuters. "I do not think he would reorganize the movement because now he is 44 and not the impetuous young man who founded the MRTA when he was 28."
